items.title: L11: Break-even, contribution and margin of safety
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Break-even questions appear in senior numerical tests because they combine several steps and tempt you into a shortcut. Fixed costs do not change with the number of units sold, for example rent, salaried staff and licences. Variable costs rise with each unit, for example materials, postage and per-case fees. The contribution per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit: it is the amount each sale contributes towards paying off fixed costs and then towards profit. Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit. At that volume, profit is exactly zero. Break-even revenue is the break-even volume multiplied by the price, or fixed costs ÷ the contribution ratio (contribution ÷ price). To find the volume needed for a target profit, add the target to the fixed costs before dividing by the contribution. The margin of safety is how far actual (or forecast) sales are above break-even, usually expressed as a percentage of actual sales, (actual − break-even) ÷ actual. A common mistake is to divide fixed costs by the price, which ignores variable costs. Another is to apply a percentage rise in variable cost to the break-even volume instead of recalculating the contribution. When several products are sold, find the average contribution per unit for the sales mix, weighting each product by its share of units, and then divide fixed costs by that average. A simple average of the contributions is wrong unless the mix is equal. Round break-even volumes up, since a part-unit cannot be sold.

questions.prompt: A service has fixed costs of £84,000 a year. Each unit sells for £35 and has variable costs of £21. How many units must be sold to break even?
questions.hint: Divide fixed costs by the contribution of £14 per unit.

questions.prompt: Using the same figures (fixed costs £84,000, price £35, variable cost £21), what is the break-even revenue?
questions.hint: Multiply break-even units by the price of £35.

questions.prompt: Fixed costs are £84,000, the price is £35 and variable cost is £21. Sales are 8,000 units. What is the profit?
questions.hint: Profit is units × contribution minus fixed costs.

questions.prompt: With sales of 8,000 units and break-even at 6,000 units, what is the margin of safety as a percentage of actual sales?
questions.hint: Divide the 2,000 units above break-even by the 8,000 actually sold.

questions.prompt: Fixed costs are £84,000 and contribution is £14 a unit. How many units must be sold to make a profit of £35,000?
questions.hint: Add the target profit to fixed costs before dividing.

questions.prompt: Variable cost per unit rises by 10%, from £21, with the price and fixed costs unchanged. To the nearest whole unit, what is the new break-even volume, rounded up?
questions.hint: The contribution falls to £11.90, so divide £84,000 by that.

questions.prompt: Fixed costs rise by £14,000 to £98,000 and the price rises to £37, with variable cost still £21. What is the new break-even volume?
questions.hint: New contribution is £16, so divide £98,000 by 16.

questions.prompt: A body sells product A (contribution £14) and product B (contribution £6) in the ratio 3 units of A to 1 unit of B. Fixed costs are £84,000. How many units in total are needed to break even?
questions.hint: The mix gives an average contribution of (3 × 14 + 6) ÷ 4 = £12.

items.title: L11: Price, volume and mix variances
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: A variance is the difference between what was planned and what actually happened. In a cost variance, spending above the plan is adverse and spending below it is favourable. For income, the signs reverse. A raw variance can mislead: if a team handled more cases than planned, spending more than budget is not necessarily overspending. The sensible comparison is against a flexed budget, which is the original budget recalculated at the actual activity level. A total cost variance can be split into two parts. The volume variance is (actual volume − budget volume) × budget price. The price variance is (actual price − budget price) × actual volume. Together they add up to the total variance. A positive price difference on costs is adverse. A third effect appears when the cost per hour differs across grades. The mix variance measures the cost of changing the proportion of hours spent at each grade, calculated as actual hours at the actual mix valued at standard rates, minus the same total hours at the planned mix. The rate variance is the difference between the actual cost and actual hours valued at standard rates. A good habit is to check your split by adding the parts to see if they equal the total. State the direction as well as the size: an answer of £1,500 without a label is incomplete. Remember also that the percentage overspend is the variance divided by the original budget, not by the actual spend.

questions.prompt: A budget planned 4,000 units at £12.50 each. Actual spending was 4,400 units at £12.90 each. What is the total cost variance?

options.text: £6,760 favourable
£1,760 adverse
£5,000 adverse
£6,760 adverse

questions.hint: Actual spend of £56,760 is above the £50,000 budget.

questions.prompt: Using the same figures, what is the volume variance (extra units at the budgeted price)?

options.text: £5,160 adverse
£1,760 adverse
£5,000 adverse
£5,000 favourable

questions.hint: 400 extra units × £12.50.

questions.prompt: Using the same figures, what is the price variance (price difference applied to the actual quantity)?

options.text: £1,600 adverse
£1,760 adverse
£1,760 favourable
£5,000 adverse

questions.hint: The price was £0.40 above budget on 4,400 units.

questions.prompt: A total cost variance is split into a volume variance of £5,000 adverse and a price variance of £1,760 adverse. The original budget was £50,000. What is the overspend as a percentage of the original budget?
questions.hint: Divide the £6,760 total by the original budget, not the actual spend.

questions.prompt: A budget was £2,400,000. The team spent £2,580,000 while handling 8% more cases than planned, with costs assumed to vary directly with cases. How does spending compare with the flexed budget?

options.text: £12,000 favourable
£12,000 adverse
£192,000 favourable
£180,000 adverse

questions.hint: The flexed budget is £2,592,000, which is above actual spend.

questions.prompt: Planned work was 1,000 hours, split 60% at £30 an hour and 40% at £40. In practice the 1,000 hours were split 45% at £30 and 55% at £40. What is the mix variance?

options.text: £35,500 adverse
£1,500 adverse
£700 adverse
£1,500 favourable

questions.hint: Compare £35,500 with £34,000 at the planned mix.

questions.prompt: In the staffing example the actual cost of the 1,000 hours was £36,200, and the hours valued at standard rates were £35,500. What is the rate variance?

options.text: £1,500 adverse
£2,200 adverse
£700 adverse
£700 favourable

questions.hint: Actual cost minus actual hours at standard rates.

questions.prompt: A unit's actual price was £12.10 against a standard of £12.50, on 4,400 units bought. What is the price variance?

options.text: £0.40 favourable
£1,760 adverse
£1,600 favourable
£1,760 favourable

questions.hint: A lower price than standard on 4,400 units is favourable.

items.title: L11: Marginal rates, thresholds and take-home pay
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Banded schemes charge different rates on different slices of a figure. The rate on the last slice is the marginal rate, while the total charged divided by the whole amount is the average rate. The average rate is always below the highest marginal rate once the top band is reached, and it rises towards it as the amount grows. In the examples below, a free allowance applies to the first £12,000. Between £12,000 and £50,000 the rate is 20%, and above £50,000 the rate is 40%. These bands are used for practice and are not the actual rates of any scheme. Method: work band by band, add the slices, and only then compute averages. To find what an extra payment yields, find which band each part of it falls into, because a rise can straddle a boundary. Deductions made before the charge, for example some pension contributions, reduce the amount that is charged. To find where the average rate reaches a stated figure, write the total charge as an expression, set it equal to the rate multiplied by the amount, and solve. Comparing a banded scheme with a flat rate often shows the flat rate costs more at low amounts and less at high amounts. Always check that the answer lies in the band you assumed. If solving gives an amount that is outside the band, your assumption was wrong and you must start again with another band.

questions.prompt: Using the practice bands (nothing on the first £12,000, 20% from £12,000 to £50,000, 40% above £50,000), what is the charge on an amount of £62,000?
questions.hint: £7,600 on the middle band plus £4,800 on the top band.

questions.prompt: On an amount of £62,000 under the practice bands, the charge is £12,400. What is the average rate?
questions.hint: Divide the total charge by the whole £62,000.

questions.prompt: An amount is £49,000. It rises by £3,000. Under the practice bands, how much of the rise is left after the extra charge?
questions.hint: £1,000 is charged at 20% and £2,000 at 40%.

questions.prompt: An amount of £48,000 rises by 5%. Under the practice bands, how much of the rise remains after the extra charge?
questions.hint: The whole £2,400 is within the 20% band.

questions.prompt: A person with £40,000 pays 8% into a scheme before the charge is applied, so the charge is based on the reduced amount. Under the practice bands, what is left after the contribution and the charge?
questions.hint: The charge is on £36,800, which is £4,960.

questions.prompt: Under the practice bands, at what amount does the average rate reach 25%? (It is in the top band.)
questions.hint: Set 0.4X − 12,400 equal to 0.25X.

questions.prompt: A flat rate of 22% is compared with the practice bands on an amount of £62,000. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The flat rate costs £1,240 more
The flat rate costs £620 more
The flat rate costs £1,240 less
The two schemes cost the same

questions.hint: A flat 22% is £13,640 against £12,400.

questions.prompt: The tax-free allowance of £12,000 rises by 5%, with the bands otherwise unchanged. How much less is charged on any amount above £12,600 that is within the 20% band?
questions.hint: The extra £600 of free allowance saves 20% of it.

items.title: L11: Rates of work, queues and staffing
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Capacity problems turn on a few relationships. Workload = number of cases × time per case. Capacity = number of staff × productive hours per person × (1 ÷ time per case). Staff are not productive for the whole of their contracted day, so questions often give productive hours (after breaks, meetings and leave). Staff needed = workload ÷ productive time per person, and part-people are rounded up because you cannot employ 8.33 people. A backlog changes by arrivals minus completions each period. If capacity exceeds arrivals, the backlog falls by the surplus; if it does not, the backlog grows and no amount of waiting will clear it. Time to clear = backlog ÷ surplus capacity, rounded up to a whole period. Absence reduces capacity in proportion: with 8% absence, only 92% of the staff are available. Process improvements change the time per case, which scales the capacity inversely, so a 20% cut in the time per case raises capacity by 25%, not 20%. Little's law says that in a steady state, the average number waiting equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average wait, so average wait = queue size ÷ arrival rate. When two teams work on a fixed job at different speeds, combine their rates: the time is the job size ÷ the sum of the rates. If one starts earlier, subtract the work it has already done first.

questions.prompt: A team receives 120 cases a day, and each takes 25 minutes. Each member has 6 productive hours a day. What is the smallest number of staff that can keep up with the arrivals?
questions.hint: The workload is 3,000 minutes, and each person gives 360, so 8.33 rounds up.

questions.prompt: With 9 staff, 6 productive hours each and 25 minutes per case, daily capacity is 129.6 cases against 120 arrivals. A backlog of 1,000 cases exists. How many whole days does it take to clear it?
questions.hint: Divide 1,000 by the daily surplus of 9.6 cases.

questions.prompt: Using 10 staff, 25 minutes a case and 6 productive hours, with 120 arrivals a day, how many days does a backlog of 1,000 cases take to clear?
questions.hint: Capacity of 144 leaves a surplus of 24 a day.

questions.prompt: The team has 10 staff but 8% are absent on average. Everything else is as before (25 minutes, 6 hours, 120 arrivals). How many days to clear 1,000 cases, rounded up?
questions.hint: Only 9.2 staff are effectively available, giving capacity of 132.48.

questions.prompt: The process is redesigned and the time per case falls by 20%, from 25 to 20 minutes. With 9 staff, 6 productive hours and 120 arrivals, how many days does it take to clear a backlog of 1,000 cases?
questions.hint: Capacity rises to 162 a day, so the surplus is 42.

questions.prompt: An average of 600 cases are waiting at any time, and 120 cases arrive each day in a steady state. By Little's law, what is the average wait?

options.text: 600 days
5 days
20 days
0.2 days

questions.hint: Average wait = queue size ÷ arrival rate.

questions.prompt: Team A completes 40 cases a day and team B 60 cases a day. A starts a job of 1,000 cases 3 days before B joins in. How many days after B joins is the job finished?

options.text: 8.8 days
10 days
5 days
7.5 days

questions.hint: A completes 120 first, then the two together manage 100 a day.

questions.prompt: A backlog is 900 cases. Arrivals are 150 a day and capacity is 140 a day. After 30 days, what is the backlog if nothing changes?
questions.hint: The backlog grows by the shortfall of 10 each day.

items.title: L11: Reading charts and tables described in words
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Some questions describe a chart in words instead of showing it, and you must rebuild the numbers before answering. Start by writing the figures down in a small table with units. A bar chart gives quantities for each category. A pie or share chart gives percentages of one total, which you must multiply by that total to find counts. Percentage change is (new − old) ÷ old, so a rise from one quarter to the next and the fall back are not the same percentage, because the base differs. Percentage points are the arithmetic difference between two percentages, while percentage change is relative to the starting percentage. A fall from 12.5% to 9% is 3.5 percentage points and a 28% fall. A share shifting from one category to another keeps the total unchanged. An average of several periods is the total divided by the number of periods, and an average of percentages is only correct if the bases are equal. When the question says 'to the nearest' or 'in thousands', check the unit before you choose. Under time pressure, estimate first: if an answer is obviously between two options, you may not need exact arithmetic. Read the axis labels in the description, as a chart whose axis starts above zero exaggerates differences. Finally, answer exactly what is asked: a count and a share of the count are different answers.

questions.prompt: A bar chart shows applications received in four quarters: Q1 4,200; Q2 4,830; Q3 5,520; Q4 4,950. What is the percentage rise from Q1 to Q3, to one decimal place?
questions.hint: Divide the rise of 1,320 by the Q1 figure.

questions.prompt: In the same chart, applications fall from 5,520 in Q3 to 4,950 in Q4. What is the percentage fall, to one decimal place?
questions.hint: Divide the fall of 570 by the Q3 figure.

questions.prompt: The four quarters total 19,500 applications. A share chart says 55% were online, 30% by post and 15% by phone. How many were made by post?

In the same year, phone applications rise by 5 percentage points as a share, taking the share from the post category only. Total applications stay at 19,500. How many applications are then made by post?
questions.hint: The post share falls from 30% to 25%.

questions.prompt: A rate falls from 12.5% to 9.0%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It has fallen by 3.5%, a relative fall of 28 percentage points
It has fallen by 3.5 percentage points, a relative fall of 28%
It has fallen by 28 percentage points, a relative fall of 3.5%
It has fallen by 3.5 percentage points, a relative fall of 38.9%

questions.hint: The difference is 3.5 points and 3.5 ÷ 12.5 is 28%.

questions.prompt: The quarterly average across the four quarters is 4,875. How does the combined total of Q2 and Q4 compare with two average quarters, in applications?

options.text: 30 below
45 below
75 above
30 above

questions.hint: 9,780 compared with 9,750.

questions.prompt: Online applications are 55% of 19,500. Of those, 20% were rejected as incomplete. How many online applications were complete?
questions.hint: Multiply 10,725 by 0.8.

questions.prompt: A chart axis for staffing numbers starts at 400 rather than at zero. The bars show 410 and 440. A report claims the second bar is 'four times as high'. Which statement about the real values is correct?

options.text: The second value is about 7% higher, not four times as high
The second value is 10% higher, because 440 is 10% above 400
The second value is about 7% lower, because the axis is truncated
The second value is four times as high, as the bars show

questions.hint: The real values are 440 and 410, not the heights above 400.

items.title: L11: Verdicts when passages compare change over time
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Passages that describe change over time give many ways to over-read. First fix the baseline and the window: 'fell in each of the last three years' tells you the direction in each year, but not how large each fall was. Next separate level from rate, and count from share. If the share of applications made online rises, the number made online may still fall when the total falls sharply, so check both parts. A percentage rise on a small base can be smaller in pounds than a lower percentage rise on a large base. When a combined figure stays the same while the mix shifts towards a slower or dearer group, at least one group must have improved, and the reverse is also true. Net change means arrivals minus departures, and a subset of leavers is already inside the leaver total, so it must not be subtracted twice. A before-and-after pattern does not show cause if the trend was already running before the change, so a passage that says a measure began in year two and shows waits falling since year one cannot prove the measure worked. Words such as 'since', 'over the period' and 'at the start of' fix the dates, so use them exactly. Where a statement says 'at least one', ask whether the figures force it. If a total is fixed and one share rises, another must fall. Choose 'cannot say' only when the passage truly leaves the answer open, and not whenever a number has to be calculated, as a verdict can often be settled by simple arithmetic on what is given.

questions.prompt: "Average waiting times for assessment were 41 days at the start of year one, then 38, 35 and 33 at the end of years one, two and three. Online booking was introduced at the start of year two." Statement: "Online booking caused the fall in waiting times in years two and three." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: the fall in year three was smaller than the fall in year one
True: waiting times fell in both years after online booking was introduced
False: waits fell by 3 days in year one, before online booking, as they did in year two
Cannot say: waits were already falling before online booking began

questions.hint: A fall that began before the change cannot be credited to the change.

questions.prompt: "Spending on training rose from £2.0m to £2.4m over two years, while spending on travel rose from £1.0m to £1.3m over the same two years." Statement: "Travel spending rose by a larger percentage than training spending." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: training rose by £400,000 against £300,000 for travel
Cannot say: the passage does not say whether the rises had been planned
True: travel rose by 30% and training by 20%
Cannot say: the passage does not give the figures for each separate year

questions.hint: Compare the percentage rises, not the pound rises.

questions.prompt: "Complaints fell in each of the last four quarters. The most recent quarter's complaints were 212." Statement: "The most recent quarter had fewer complaints than any of the previous four quarters." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: True: a fall in every quarter means the latest figure is the lowest of the run
False: complaints in earlier years may have been lower still
Cannot say: 212 might not be low compared with the national total
Cannot say: the size of each quarterly fall is not given

questions.hint: Each quarter below the one before makes the last the lowest.

questions.prompt: "The share of applications made online rose from 40% to 52%, while total applications fell from 50,000 to 45,000." Statement: "The number of applications made online rose." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: total applications fell, so online applications must have fallen too
True: online applications went from 20,000 to 23,400
True: the share rose by 12 points, so online applications rose by 12%
Cannot say: the passage gives only shares, not the number made online

questions.hint: Multiply each share by its own total before comparing.

questions.prompt: "Average processing time was 12 days in January and 12 days in June. Between those months the mix of work shifted towards complex cases, which take longer to process than simple cases in both months." Statement: "Neither type of case was processed faster in June than in January." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: with more of the slower work and an unchanged average, some type must have got faster
Cannot say: the processing time for each type of case is not given
True: the average processing time did not change between the two months
Cannot say: the passage does not say how many cases were handled in each month

questions.hint: Unchanged times with a worse mix would have raised the average.

questions.prompt: "A department began the year with 1,200 staff. During the year it recruited 150 people and lost 90, of whom 30 left to join other departments." Statement: "The department's headcount rose by 60 over the year." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not give the closing headcount
Cannot say: transfers in from other departments are not mentioned
False: the 30 transfers must be taken off as well, giving a rise of 30
True: the 90 leavers already include the 30 transfers, so the net rise is 60

questions.hint: A subset of the leavers is already counted in the 90.

questions.prompt: "In 2021 a unit closed 80% of its 3,000 cases within target. In 2022 it closed 84% of its 2,500 cases within target." Statement: "More cases were closed within target in 2022 than in 2021." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: True: the rate within target improved from 80% to 84%
False: 2,100 cases in 2022 against 2,400 in 2021
Cannot say: the cases that missed target are not itemised
True: the improvement was 4 percentage points on each case

questions.hint: The caseload fell by more than the rate improved.

questions.prompt: "Three regional offices handled 40%, 35% and 25% of all cases last year. Office C's share rose to 30% this year, and the total number of cases did not change." Statement: "At least one of the other two offices handled fewer cases this year than last year." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: True: the other two offices must have lost exactly the same number of cases
Cannot say: the passage does not say how C's gain was split between A and B
True: with the total fixed, C's gain must come from A, B or both
False: the passage does not say that either office lost cases

questions.hint: If one share rises and the total is fixed, another falls.

items.title: L11: Flaws in an argument: straw men, false dilemmas and circles
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Reasoning tests often ask you to name what is wrong with an argument. The commonest flaws have stable names and can be recognised by structure. A false dilemma offers two options as if no others existed, such as 'ban consultants or accept spiralling costs', when capping, scoping or monitoring would be possible. A straw man misrepresents an opponent's position in a weaker or more extreme form and then attacks that version. Circular reasoning uses the conclusion as a reason for itself, so the argument goes nowhere. An ad hominem dismisses a claim because of who made it, instead of examining the claim, though a relevant conflict of interest may rightly make you check more carefully. Hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from a few or unrepresentative cases. Appeal to popularity claims something is right or best because many people do it. A slippery slope says one step will inevitably lead to an extreme end without showing the links. Equivocation uses a word in two senses within one argument so that the conclusion appears to follow. A good method is to state the argument in three parts: the claim, the reason and the link between them. Then ask whether the link is missing, circular or switches meaning. A flawed argument can have a true conclusion, so a flaw means the reasoning does not establish it, not that the conclusion is false. Keep the question in mind: is the problem with the facts, or the reasoning from them?

questions.prompt: "Either we ban all external consultants from the programme, or we accept that its costs will spiral out of control." What is the main flaw?

options.text: It relies on one example of a consultant overspending to condemn all of them
It assumes that spiralling costs are certain to follow from using consultants
It attacks the consultants themselves instead of discussing their work
It offers two options as the only ones, ignoring limits, scoping or monitoring

questions.hint: The argument ignores middle options.

questions.prompt: A minister proposes shorter application forms. A critic replies: "So the minister wants to scrap all checks on applicants. That would let anyone in." What is the flaw?

options.text: It uses the same claim as both its reason and its conclusion
It offers only two options when more are available
It misstates the proposal as something more extreme and then attacks that version
It dismisses the proposal because of who made it

questions.hint: Shorter forms do not mean no checks.

questions.prompt: "The review panel is fair because its decisions are just. And we know its decisions are just because the panel is fair." What is the flaw?

options.text: The argument uses the word 'fair' in two different senses
Each claim is used to support the other, so neither is independently supported
The argument draws a general rule from a single decision
The argument offers two options when there are more

questions.hint: The conclusion appears in the premise.

questions.prompt: "The audit figures cannot be trusted, because the auditor once worked for a supplier." The figures themselves are not queried. What is the best description of the flaw?

options.text: It rejects the figures because of the auditor, not because anything is wrong with them
It treats a rare case as if it were typical of all audits
It assumes that the figures are right because many auditors agree
It presents the figures as the only possible measure of performance

questions.hint: The claim should be tested on its evidence.

questions.prompt: "The pilot in our twelve-person office cut errors by a third, so the whole department will see the same fall." What is the main weakness?

options.text: It treats two options as the only ones available
It dismisses other offices because of who works in them
It generalises from one small office that may not be typical of the department
It assumes that errors are caused by staff and not by systems

questions.hint: A small pilot may not represent the whole.

questions.prompt: "Most other departments use this software, so it must be the best option for ours." What is the flaw?

options.text: It misrepresents what the department's staff have asked for
Widespread use is treated as proof of quality and of fit, without looking at our needs
The argument is circular, since use is its own reason
It offers only two options when several are available

questions.hint: Popularity is not evidence of suitability.

questions.prompt: "If we allow one team a flexible start time, soon every team will demand it, then nobody will be in during core hours and the service will collapse." What is the flaw?

options.text: It accepts the opinion of a few people as a general rule
It uses a word with two different meanings in the argument
It argues that the policy is wrong because of who proposed it
It claims a chain of events will follow without showing that each step must happen

questions.hint: Each step in the chain needs support.

questions.prompt: "The policy aims at equality. Equality means treating everyone in exactly the same way. So giving adjustments to disabled staff breaches the policy." What is the main flaw?

options.text: 'Equality' is used in two senses, so the conclusion does not follow
The argument offers only two options when others exist
The argument supports its conclusion by repeating it in other words
The argument attacks the people who wrote the policy

questions.hint: A shifting meaning of a key word breaks the logic.

items.title: L11: Reasoning across two sources that seem to conflict
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Officials often have to reconcile two reports, surveys or briefs that appear to disagree. The first move is to check that the two sources measure the same thing. One may count totals and the other rates; one may use a sample of volunteers and the other a random sample; one may cover a different period or define a term more narrowly. Many apparent conflicts disappear when the measures are aligned. Where a figure is given as a rate, multiply it by the relevant base before comparing it with a count. Where two multipliers are applied in sequence, multiply them: a 20% fall in average time and a 25% rise in volume give 0.8 × 1.25 = 1.0, so total time is unchanged. Percentages of percentages can be combined as fractions: two thirds supporting among the 30% who responded is 20% of everyone invited. Be careful with self-selection: if people choose to attend a workshop, those who attend may already be more motivated, so higher success among attendees does not show that the workshop caused it. Words such as 'largest single share' do not mean 'majority', but they do rule out any other category being bigger. When two figures cannot both be literally true, say so; when they could both be true under some reading, 'cannot say' is usually right. Never assume that two sources contradict each other unless both are pinned to the same population, period and definition.

questions.prompt: Source A: "The pilot cut average call time by 20%." Source B: "Call volumes in the pilot area rose by a quarter over the same period." Statement: "Total time spent on calls in the pilot area fell." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: 0.8 × 1.25 = 1, so total time was unchanged
True: the average time per call fell by 20%
Cannot say: the length of the pilot is not given
True: a 20% fall outweighs a 25% rise in volume

questions.hint: Multiply the two factors, and do not subtract them.

questions.prompt: Source A: "A survey of 400 staff found that 70% were satisfied." Source B: "Only staff who had served for more than a year were surveyed." Statement: "70% of all staff are satisfied." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: True: a sample of 400 is large enough to speak for all staff
Cannot say: the survey left out staff with under a year's service, who may differ
False: 30% of those surveyed were not satisfied
True: those with more than a year's service are the most informed

questions.hint: The sample covers only part of the staff.

questions.prompt: Source A: "Region X recorded the highest number of complaints of any region." Source B: "Region X's complaints per 1,000 users were below the national average." Statement: "Region X has a larger user population than at least one other region." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: a lower complaints rate means that the region has fewer users
Cannot say: the numbers of users in each region are not given
Cannot say: the two sources may cover different periods
True: a region above the average rate with fewer complaints must have fewer users

questions.hint: A region above the average rate with fewer complaints must be smaller.

questions.prompt: Source A: "In 2019, most detected fraud was found by internal audit." Source B: "In 2023, tip-offs from staff accounted for the largest single share of detected fraud." Statement: "In 2023, internal audit found less than half of detected fraud." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: 'largest single share' means more than half of the fraud
False: most fraud was found by internal audit in 2019 and this is unlikely to have changed
True: audit's share is below the largest, and two shares cannot both top half
Cannot say: the passage does not give 2023's figures for internal audit

questions.hint: The largest share beats audit's share, and both cannot exceed 50%.

questions.prompt: Source A: "Applicants who attended the workshop were twice as likely to be successful." Source B: "Attendance at the workshop was voluntary." Statement: "The workshop doubled applicants' chances of success." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: True: attendees were twice as likely to succeed
True: a voluntary workshop attracts those who need it most
False: attendance was voluntary, so the workshop had no effect
Cannot say: volunteers may have been more motivated or better prepared before attending

questions.hint: People choosing to attend may differ from those who do not.

questions.prompt: Source A: "The budget for the programme was £5m." Source B: "The programme overspent its budget by 12%." Statement: "The programme cost more than £5.5m." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the final cost of the programme is not stated
True: a 12% overspend on £5m is £600,000, making the cost £5.6m
False: the cost was £5.12m, as the overspend was 12p in the pound
False: 12% of £5m is £500,000, so the cost was exactly £5.5m

questions.hint: Work out 112% of £5m.

questions.prompt: Source A: "Two thirds of respondents supported the plan." Source B: "The response rate was 30%." Statement: "Fewer than a quarter of everyone invited both responded and supported the plan." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the number of people invited is not given
False: two thirds is well above a quarter
True: two thirds of 30% is 20% of everyone invited
False: 30% responded and two thirds of that is 30%

questions.hint: Fractions of fractions can be multiplied without the base.

questions.prompt: Source A: "No department exceeded its pay budget this year." Source B: "Department Q's total spending on staff was more than it planned." Statement: "The two sources contradict each other." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: spending on staff may include items that sit outside the pay budget
True: Q cannot both stay within the pay budget and spend more than planned on staff
False: the sources cover the same period, so they must agree
False: the sources cover different departments

questions.hint: The terms 'pay budget' and 'spending on staff' may not be the same measure.

items.title: L11: Deadlines, working days and sequences in prose
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000 (time limits), GOV.UK guidance on working days and bank holidays
items.body: Many rules set deadlines in working days, and a single mis-count can mean a breach. A working day is a normal weekday that is not a public holiday, and England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not always share the same holidays, so check which applies. Statutory deadlines such as the 20-working-day limit for answering a freedom of information request are normally counted from the working day after receipt, so the day of receipt is not counted as day one. Where a rule says that a request received after a cut-off time is treated as received on the next working day, apply that first, then count. When a rule lets the clock stop, for example while the department asks the requester to clarify what they want, count the days used before the stop, pause, and restart from the day after the clarification arrives. 'Within 10 working days' includes day 10 as the last allowable day. 'At least five working days before a meeting' means working backwards, excluding the meeting day itself. In practice, write the calendar out, mark weekends and holidays, and tick off each day. For sequences described in words, such as approval before spending and spending before reporting, build a chain and check that each statement fits it. If the passage says nothing about what happens in a given case, the right verdict is usually 'cannot say'. The examples below use stated rules and are for practice.

questions.prompt: A rule says: "A reply is due within 10 working days of receipt, counting from the day after receipt. Weekends and public holidays are not working days." A request is received on Wednesday 5th in a 31-day month, with no public holidays. When is the reply due?

options.text: Monday 17th
Friday 14th
Wednesday 19th
Thursday 18th

questions.hint: Count 10 weekdays starting from Thursday 6th.

questions.prompt: Under the same rule (10 working days from the day after receipt), the request was received on Wednesday 5th, but Monday 17th is a public holiday. When is the reply due?

options.text: Friday 21st
Thursday 20th
Tuesday 18th
Wednesday 19th

questions.hint: The holiday is skipped, so everything after it moves back a day.

questions.prompt: A rule says: "Requests received after 17:30 are treated as received on the next working day. A reply is due within 10 working days, counting from the day after receipt." A request is emailed at 17:45 on Friday 7th. When is the reply due?

options.text: Friday 21st
Thursday 20th
Tuesday 25th
Monday 24th

questions.hint: The request is treated as received on Monday 10th.

questions.prompt: A rule says: "The clock stops when the department asks the requester to clarify and restarts on the day after the clarification is received. A reply is due within 10 working days, counting from the day after receipt." A request is received on Monday 1st, the department asks for clarification on Thursday 4th, and the clarification arrives on Monday 8th. When is the reply due?

options.text: Wednesday 17th
Tuesday 16th
Friday 12th
Thursday 18th

questions.hint: Three working days are used before the stop and seven remain after Monday 8th.

questions.prompt: Papers must be circulated "no later than the fifth working day before the meeting". The meeting is on Monday 24th, with no public holidays. By when must the papers be circulated?

options.text: Monday 17th
Wednesday 19th
Tuesday 18th
Friday 14th

questions.hint: Count back Friday 21st as day one.

questions.prompt: "A reply is due within 10 working days of receipt, counting from the day after receipt. Weekends and public holidays are not working days." A reply was sent on Friday 14th to a request received on Wednesday 5th. Statement: "The reply was sent within the deadline." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: nine calendar days is too many for a ten-day limit
False: the day of receipt counts as day one, so the reply was late
Cannot say: the passage does not give the time the reply was sent
True: Friday 14th was the seventh working day after receipt

questions.hint: The deadline is Wednesday 19th, so this reply was early.

questions.prompt: "Approval must come before spending. Spending must come before reporting. Reporting happens once a quarter." Statement: "Approval can be given after the first report is made." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: True: reporting is quarterly, so approval can be fitted in between reports
Cannot say: the passage does not give the date of the first report
False: the first report follows spending, which in turn follows approval
True: approval is needed only once the spending has been checked

questions.hint: The chain forces approval first.

questions.prompt: "Working days exclude weekends and public holidays. Requests are due within 10 working days of receipt." A request arrived on a public holiday. Statement: "The 10 working days start counting from the day of that public holiday." Which verdict is correct?

options.text: False: no day that is not a working day can be counted
Cannot say: the passage does not say when a request received on a holiday is treated as received
True: the rule says that requests are due 10 days after receipt
False: the clock always starts on the next working day, as with weekends

questions.hint: The passage does not cover this case.

items.title: L11: Purpose, tone and the role of a sentence
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Some verbal questions ask what a writer is trying to do, not only what the passage says. Purpose is the job of the whole passage: to inform, to persuade, to warn, to recommend, to defend a decision or to evaluate options. Tone is the writer's attitude, such as neutral, cautious, critical, sceptical or enthusiastic, and is shown by word choice. Hedging words, for example 'may', 'appears' and 'on the evidence so far', signal caution. Strong words, for example 'clearly' and 'plainly', signal advocacy, and the writer may be claiming more than the evidence supports. Each sentence also has a role: a claim, the evidence for it, a counter-argument, a concession, an example or a recommendation. 'However' and 'although' often flag a counter-claim, and 'therefore' and 'so' flag a conclusion. A concession admits a point against the writer's own side, and the writer then argues it does not defeat the main claim. To test what role a sentence plays, remove it in your head and ask what the argument loses: if the conclusion loses its support, the sentence was evidence; if only the colour changes, it was an illustration. Distinguish statements of fact (checkable), opinion (a judgement), forecast (about the future) and assumption (taken for granted). A forecast cannot be shown true now, and a statement of fact can still be false. Choose the option that matches the passage's actual weight and not the loudest phrase in it.

questions.prompt: "The pilot reduced average waiting times, although only three offices took part. Even so, these early results are encouraging and justify a wider trial, provided costs are monitored." What is the author's main purpose?

options.text: To compare the costs of three different offices
To warn that the pilot should be stopped
To prove that the pilot works everywhere
To recommend a wider trial while acknowledging the limits of the evidence

questions.hint: The passage concedes limits and then recommends a trial.

questions.prompt: "The data may suggest that remote working has helped retention, but the figures are early and drawn from one department." Which word best describes the tone?

options.text: Cautious
Enthusiastic
Dismissive
Hostile

questions.hint: Hedging words such as 'may' and 'early' signal caution.

questions.prompt: "Plainly, the old system failed. It was slow, it lost records, and staff avoided using it." In the passage, what role does the sentence 'It was slow, it lost records, and staff avoided using it' play?

options.text: It states a conclusion drawn from the opening claim
It concedes a point against the writer's argument
It provides reasons in support of the opening claim
It introduces an unrelated example

questions.hint: The final sentence backs up 'the old system failed'.

questions.prompt: "Many staff prefer office working. However, a recent survey showed that productivity was unaffected by location. Therefore the department should allow flexibility." Which sentence is the main conclusion?

options.text: Many staff prefer office working
The department should allow flexibility
A recent survey was carried out
Productivity was unaffected by location

questions.hint: 'Therefore' marks the conclusion.

questions.prompt: "The new portal will be popular, and it will save at least £2m a year." Which statement describes the sentence correctly?

options.text: It is a forecast, so it cannot be shown to be true or false yet
It is an assumption stated as a premise of an earlier argument
It is a concession to the opposing view
It is a fact, because it uses a precise figure

questions.hint: Claims about the future are forecasts, however precise.

questions.prompt: "The minister's decision was wrong. It ignored the evidence and delayed help for those who needed it." Which part is an opinion?

options.text: The decision ignored the evidence
The decision was wrong
The decision was made by the minister
The decision delayed help

questions.hint: A judgement of 'wrong' is an opinion even if supported.

questions.prompt: "Some argue that the scheme costs too much. The cost is high, and no one should pretend otherwise. But it prevents far greater costs later." What does the writer do with the sentence 'The cost is high, and no one should pretend otherwise'?

options.text: Introduces an unrelated example
Restates the writer's conclusion
Gives evidence that the scheme should be dropped
Concedes a point to the critics before arguing that it does not decide the matter

questions.hint: A concession is followed by 'but'.

questions.prompt: "Clearly, the reforms are working. Every indicator is moving in the right direction." What is the most reasonable comment on the tone?

options.text: It is hostile to those who disagree
It is cautious and hedged throughout
It is confident and may claim more than the evidence supports
It is neutral and avoids taking a view

questions.hint: 'Clearly' and 'every' signal strong claims.

items.title: L11: Working with a minister's private office
items.source: Civil Service Code, Ministerial Code and the Code of Conduct for Special Advisers, GOV.UK
items.body: Ministers are supported by a private office staffed by civil servants, often with a private secretary leading it. The office manages the minister's diary, correspondence, submissions and requests for briefing. Officials in policy and delivery teams work with it every day, and the relationship works best when both sides are clear, quick and honest. Submissions (the formal written advice to a minister) usually set out the issue, the recommendation, the options considered, the risks, the financial and legal implications and the handling, and they should be accurate, balanced and as short as the decision allows. The minister decides; officials advise, and their advice must be impartial, honest and based on evidence, even when it is unwelcome. Special advisers are political appointees who are temporary civil servants under their own Code of Conduct. They may ask for work and policy advice on behalf of their minister, but they must not be allowed to manage permanent civil servants or to ask officials to act in a way that breaches the Civil Service Code. Deadlines from the private office are often tight. The right response to an unrealistic deadline is to say early what can be done and when, and what the trade-offs are, and not to deliver rushed or unchecked work. Briefing for Parliament and the press must be accurate and consistent with what has been said before. If you find a mistake in material already given to the minister, tell the private office promptly so that it can be corrected. Keep a clear record of what was asked and what was decided, particularly when advice is not taken, and escalate concerns through your line management.

questions.prompt: A private secretary asks your team for a submission by 4pm today. You can have a sound draft by tomorrow morning but not today. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask your own line manager to refuse the request on your behalf because the notice is too short
Work towards 4pm and tell the private office only if the deadline is going to be missed
Tell the private office now what you can deliver and when
Send a rushed draft at 4pm and flag in the covering note that it may contain errors

questions.hint: Early, honest communication lets the office manage the minister's diary.

questions.prompt: The minister prefers option C, but your analysis shows option B is better value and carries lower risk. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Recommend B but tell the press office that officials disagree with the minister's choice
Recommend B with reasons, set out C fairly, and implement the decision
Leave B out of the submission so that the minister is not put in an awkward position
Present only option C, as it is the minister's known preference and avoids friction

questions.hint: Officials give honest advice, and the minister decides.

questions.prompt: A special adviser tells a member of your team to change the wording of a factual table so that results appear better than the data show. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Make the change, since special advisers speak with the minister's authority
Ignore the request and say nothing to anyone, hoping it will not be raised again
Make the change but add a small footnote saying that the table has been reworded
Decline to alter the facts, explain why, and tell your line manager

questions.hint: The Civil Service Code requires honesty and objectivity.

questions.prompt: After a submission has gone to the minister, you spot a figure that is wrong by a material amount. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the private office straight away and give the correct figure
Correct the figure in the next submission without drawing attention to the earlier one
Wait until the minister has decided and then explain that the figure was wrong
Wait to see whether anyone notices the error before deciding what to do

questions.hint: Errors in advice must be corrected promptly.

questions.prompt: A minister's office asks for a draft answer to a parliamentary question. The draft that is wanted would be technically accurate but would leave a misleading impression. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Draft it as wanted and warn a journalist you know that it could be misread
Decline to provide any draft and tell the private office to write it themselves
Draft what is wanted, since every statement in it is technically accurate
Draft an answer that is accurate and not misleading, and explain why

questions.hint: Answers to Parliament must be accurate and not misleading.

questions.prompt: Several private office staff chase you at the same time for the same briefing, each with different requests. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Prepare separate versions for each person who asks so that everyone is satisfied
Agree one point of contact and confirm a single timetable
Prepare only the first request received and ignore the others until they chase
Ask each person to settle it among themselves without involving you in the discussion

questions.hint: Clarify the request and the owner before spending effort.

questions.prompt: The minister decides against your recommendation and asks you to take the work forward. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Pass the work to a colleague so that you do not have to implement it yourself
Carry out the decision but tell colleagues privately that you disagree with it
Record the advice and decision, then carry it out in full
Delay the work while you ask the minister to reconsider the decision once more

questions.hint: Officials must carry out lawful decisions of ministers.

questions.prompt: The private office asks you to leave a known risk out of a submission, because the minister 'does not like bad news'. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Explain that it must be included, and offer to present it concisely
Leave it out but raise it orally if the minister asks about the risks
Leave it out and add it to a later submission once the decision is made
Put it in an annex where the minister is unlikely to look

questions.hint: Complete, honest advice is part of the job.

items.title: L11: Managing a team under sustained pressure
items.source: HSE Management Standards for work-related stress and Civil Service People Plan guidance
items.body: A manager responsible for a team under long periods of pressure must balance delivery against the wellbeing of their staff, as the employer has a legal duty of care for health and safety, including work-related stress. The Health and Safety Executive's Management Standards identify six areas that cause stress when they go wrong: demands (workload and pace), control (say over how work is done), support (from managers and colleagues), relationships (including bullying and conflict), role (clarity of what is expected) and change (how it is communicated and managed). Managers who see signs, such as increased sickness, withdrawal, irritability, mistakes or long hours, should talk to the person in private, listen without judging, and look for practical adjustments. Teams cannot do everything at once, so prioritisation is central: separate what is urgent from what is important, agree with your own manager what will not be done or will be delayed, and make the trade-offs visible. Redistributing work fairly, stopping low-value tasks, borrowing capacity from other teams and asking for more resource are better than simply asking people to do more. Heroic overtime is a short-term fix, not a plan, and managers should avoid praising long hours as a norm. Staff should know about the Employee Assistance Programme and about reasonable adjustments, and managers should model good practice by taking leave themselves. Regular check-ins, honest updates and recognition of effort help sustain morale. Decisions on workload should be recorded so that they can be justified later.

questions.prompt: Your team has had three months of heavy workload and two of its members are now showing signs of strain. A new urgent request arrives. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give the request to the staff member who copes best under pressure and keep the rest steady
Say nothing about it and wait to see whether another team picks it up
Accept the request and ask the whole team to work longer hours until it is done
Agree with your manager what can be delayed or stopped, and be honest with the team

questions.hint: Prioritise and renegotiate, rather than adding to the load.

questions.prompt: A reliable team member who has always been cheerful has become withdrawn and is making errors. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Arrange a private, supportive conversation and agree practical help
Give them a formal warning because the standard of their work has dropped
Raise the dip in quality at the next team meeting as a general reminder to everyone
Leave them alone until they bring the matter up themselves, to respect their privacy

questions.hint: Early, private support is better than waiting or penalising.

questions.prompt: One team member regularly stays late and sends emails at midnight, and colleagues feel they must do the same. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Praise their commitment in the team meeting as an example for others to follow
Talk to them about sustainable hours and say that long hours are not expected
Tell the rest of the team to ignore the late emails and carry on as normal
Do nothing, because they are choosing to work these hours of their own accord

questions.hint: Managers shape the culture around hours.

questions.prompt: You cannot deliver all five priorities set by your director with your current staff. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Try to deliver all five and accept that the quality of each will fall
Quietly decide which two to drop and tell nobody until they are missed
Show your director what is achievable and ask them to decide which to defer
Ask the team to choose the priorities between themselves and report back

questions.hint: Trade-offs belong with whoever sets the priorities.

questions.prompt: Two staff are on long-term sickness absence and the remaining team are covering their work. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Remove absent staff from team communications so that they can rest properly
Divide all of the absent colleagues' work equally between the team and carry on
Reallocate or stop tasks fairly, seek cover, and keep in contact with absent colleagues
Ask the team to cover the work without telling them how long it will last

questions.hint: Cover must be planned, fair and time-limited.

questions.prompt: In a one-to-one, a team member says that their role is unclear and they are being given conflicting instructions by two managers. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Clarify their role with the other manager, then confirm it in writing
Tell them to follow whichever instruction they received most recently
Ask them to resolve the conflict themselves directly with the other manager
Tell them that this is part of working in a busy department and carry on

questions.hint: Role clarity is one of the six stress factors.

questions.prompt: The team has just met a big deadline after weeks of strain. Another piece of work is due to start next week. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give everyone a week off without checking the work plan against deadlines
Move straight on to the next piece of work and thank them afterwards
Send a thank-you email and make no change to the workload ahead
Thank them, allow recovery time, and plan the next work sustainably

questions.hint: Recovery and recognition help to sustain performance.

questions.prompt: A team member asks for a reduction in workload for health reasons, and gives you a doctor's note. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them that everyone is under pressure and nobody gets a lighter load
Discuss reasonable adjustments, seek occupational health advice and record what is agreed
Pass the matter to HR and take no further part in discussions about the workload
Grant the reduction informally and tell nobody else, to keep it private

questions.hint: A manager should explore adjustments and record them.

items.title: L11: Conflicting priorities from senior stakeholders
items.source: Civil Service Code and Civil Service Leadership Statement, GOV.UK
items.body: Mid-level managers often receive instructions from more than one senior person who have different priorities, for example a director who wants a project delivered fast and a finance lead who wants spending controlled. The Civil Service Leadership Statement stresses being inspiring, confident, empowering, and open and transparent about decisions. The practical steps are clear. First, make sure that you understand each request: what outcome is wanted, by when, and what 'good' looks like. Second, check whether the conflict is real. Often the two aims can both be met with a small change in scope or timing. Third, if the conflict is real, do not decide it quietly by favouring the more senior or the more forceful person. Make the trade-off visible to both and, if necessary, take it to the person who can arbitrate, usually your shared line manager or the senior responsible owner of the programme. Fourth, bring options and a recommendation, and not just the problem. Fifth, keep a record of the decision and the reasons, so that those who made it can be held to account and the team knows what to do. Avoid telling each stakeholder only what they want to hear. Avoid ignoring one request and hoping that it will go away. If you are told to do something that breaches the Civil Service Code, the conflict is no longer about priorities but about propriety, and it should be raised through the proper route. Where a request breaks rules on spending, use the finance and propriety guidance, and ask for the instruction in writing.

questions.prompt: A director asks you to speed up delivery by cutting testing, while the finance lead asks you to cut spending and keep the original date. You cannot do both. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Set out options and risks for both and ask your shared senior to decide
Tell each of them what they want to hear and decide which to follow later
Follow the director's instruction, as it is more senior and the date is fixed
Satisfy the finance lead, because spending control is non-negotiable

questions.hint: Make a real conflict visible to the person who can arbitrate.

questions.prompt: Two senior colleagues give you apparently opposed instructions, but you suspect they are talking about different aspects of the same work. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the team to guess which one is more urgent and start there
Assume that they mean the same thing and do whatever is simplest
Do what the more forceful of the two asked and update the other later
Check each request and its purpose with both of them

questions.hint: First check whether the conflict is real.

questions.prompt: You agree a recommendation on a trade-off but your director then changes their mind and tells you to go with their original preference. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the finance lead that the director has overruled your recommendation
Record the decision and reasons, then carry on and raise serious risks properly
Slow the work to a halt until the director confirms the change again
Carry on with your original plan and say nothing about the change in direction

questions.hint: Decisions should be recorded, and risks escalated properly.

questions.prompt: A senior stakeholder repeatedly adds work to your team's plan without taking anything out. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ignore the new requests and see whether the stakeholder chases them
Add the work but let the quality slide a little, which no one will notice
Show them the capacity picture and agree what to drop or delay
Add it all and ask the team to work longer hours until the peak has passed

questions.hint: Added work needs agreed trade-offs.

questions.prompt: A programme board member asks you privately to hold back information about a delay from the rest of the board. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Hold it back for a week while the board member tries to solve the issue
Explain that the board needs accurate information and offer a joint briefing
Tell the board but say that the delay was caused by your own team
Tell the other members informally in the corridor and not at the meeting

questions.hint: Openness and honesty apply to all stakeholders.

questions.prompt: A very senior official tells you to bypass the normal procurement approval to save time. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Carry it out but keep a private note in case problems arise later
Refuse without giving a reason and leave the matter there
Carry out the instruction, because it comes from someone far more senior
Say approval must follow the rules, ask for it in writing and seek advice

questions.hint: A request to bypass controls is a propriety issue.

questions.prompt: You have time to deliver only one of two requests this week. One is from a director, and the other is from a junior colleague, but the junior's request supports a statutory deadline. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Do the director's work, because seniority is what sets the priorities
Do half of each so that neither person can say you ignored them
Weigh impact and consequences, and tell the director the trade-off
Do the junior colleague's work and tell nobody that you made a choice

questions.hint: Priorities should reflect impact and deadlines, not rank.

questions.prompt: After a decision has been made on a conflict between two stakeholders, one of them continues to lobby your team to reverse it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Explain the decision and its reasons, and refer them to the decision-maker
Reopen the decision to keep the stakeholder happy and avoid further calls
Tell them that someone else made the decision and that you do not agree with it
Ask your team to avoid taking their calls until they stop lobbying

questions.hint: Decisions should be supported and challenge routed properly.

items.title: L11: Correcting errors in published or briefed information
items.source: Ministerial Code, Civil Service Code and Code of Practice for Statistics, GOV.UK
items.body: Sooner or later every department finds an error in something it has said or published: a figure in a briefing, a statement in a press release or a published statistic. How it responds shows its integrity. The Civil Service Code requires officials to be honest, and the Ministerial Code says that it is of paramount importance that ministers give accurate and truthful information to Parliament, correcting any inadvertent error at the earliest opportunity. The Code of Practice for Statistics requires producers of official statistics to be open about errors, to correct them promptly and visibly, and to explain what has changed. The usual sequence is: confirm the error and its scale, tell the people who need to know (your line manager, the private office, the press office and the owner of the data), correct the source and any copies, tell users who relied on the figure, and review how it happened so that it does not recur. Speed matters, but so does accuracy of the correction, so check that the replacement figure is right before publishing it. A correction should be visible, dated and clear about what changed. It should not be hidden in a footnote or slipped quietly into a later release. Where the error could affect decisions, such as funding allocations, tell those affected directly. Do not blame individuals in public; look at systems and checking. A culture in which people can report mistakes without fear is the best defence, because errors that are reported early are smaller and cheaper to fix.

questions.prompt: You find that a published statistic was overstated by a material amount owing to a spreadsheet error. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Fix the figure in the next scheduled release and say nothing about the earlier one
Wait until someone outside the department queries the figure
Quietly replace the figure on the website without adding any note
Confirm the error, tell your manager and publish a clear correction

questions.hint: Errors in official statistics should be corrected visibly and promptly.

questions.prompt: A minister has told Parliament a figure that you now know to be wrong because of an error by your team. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the minister to say that the original figure was a rounding difference
Wait for the next parliamentary question to include the right figure naturally
Tell the private office at once and support correcting the record
Tell the minister only if the figure is queried by another member

questions.hint: Ministers must correct inadvertent errors at the earliest opportunity.

questions.prompt: Before you publish a correction, you realise that your corrected figure might also be wrong. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Check the corrected figure first, and warn stakeholders a correction is coming
Publish the correction together with a note that a further error is possible
Publish it straight away, since speed matters more than accuracy
Delay everything until the full review of the whole dataset is complete

questions.hint: A correction must itself be right.

questions.prompt: A local authority has used your incorrect figure to set its budget. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the authority to change its budget without explaining the reason why
Contact them directly, explain the error and discuss its effect
Rely on the website correction and wait to be contacted by anyone affected
Wait to see whether the authority notices that the figure has changed

questions.hint: Those who relied on the figure should be told directly.

questions.prompt: The error was caused by a junior analyst who followed an unclear procedure. A colleague suggests naming them in the correction notice. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Name the analyst, so that people know where the responsibility lies
Explain the error without naming them, and fix the procedure and checks
Say it was a system failure, without checking
Leave the notice vague and not mention a cause

questions.hint: Focus on systems and learning, not blame.

questions.prompt: A press officer wants to describe a correction as a 'minor update'. The change is large. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Agree, since a calmer description will limit press interest
Leave the decision to the press officer
Agree, but leave the full details to the footnotes
Advise that the notice should say plainly what has changed and by how much

questions.hint: Corrections should be clear about what changed.

questions.prompt: You notice that a briefing you wrote last month contained a small mistake that has not so far been used in any decision. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the people who hold the briefing, and issue a corrected version
Wait until the next version of the briefing
Say nothing, because it was not used
Update your own copy and keep the original in the file

questions.hint: Tell people, even if the mistake is small and has not caused harm yet.

questions.prompt: After a significant error is corrected, the team is nervous and reluctant to report problems in future. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Skip a review so that the team can move on quickly and forget the matter
Move the analyst concerned to another team to stop it happening again
Run a blame-free review, share lessons and welcome early reporting
Tell everyone that no more errors will be acceptable in future

questions.hint: A culture of reporting is the best protection.
